learnerMaterial.title: Specify a Sequence of Rigid Transformations
learnerMaterial.subject: mathematics
learnerMaterial.lessonGoal: Describe a sequence of rigid transformations precisely enough that another person can reproduce and verify the image.
successCriteria: I name each transformation and its defining information.
I apply transformations in the stated order.
I verify preserved distance and angle measures.
keyPoints: A transformation sequence is composition: order matters.
A translation needs a vector, a rotation needs a center and angle, and a reflection needs a line.
Rigid motions preserve distances and angle measures.

vocabulary.definition: applying transformations in sequence, using each image as the next input

sections.title: Track every vertex
sections.body: Triangle A(1,1), B(3,1), C(1,2) is translated by ⟨2,−1⟩, then rotated 90° counterclockwise about the origin.

sections.title: Worked example: write a reproducible sequence
sections.directions: Study the completed sequence and its check.

items.prompt: Describe the transformation from the original triangle to the final image in the table.

steps: Translate every point 2 units right and 1 unit down: (x,y) → (x+2,y−1).
Rotate the translated image 90° counterclockwise about (0,0): (x,y) → (−y,x).
Keep the order: rotation first would produce different coordinates.
Check AB: its length is 2 at the start and 2 in the final image, as required for rigid motions.

items.prompt: Point P(2,−1) is translated by ⟨−3,4⟩, then reflected across the x-axis. Enter the final ordered pair.

feedback.correct: You used the translated point as the input to the reflection.
feedback.incorrect: Record the intermediate point first. Reflection across the x-axis keeps x and negates y.

items.prompt: Describe a rotation that maps Q(4,1) to Q′(−1,4). Include the center, angle, and direction.

feedback.correct: Your description contains enough information to reproduce the rotation.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the coordinate rule with standard rotations about the origin, then name angle and direction explicitly.

items.prompt: Explain why translating by ⟨3,0⟩ and then reflecting across the y-axis is not generally the same as doing those steps in reverse.

feedback.correct: You treated order as part of the transformation and supported the claim with a coordinate or example.
feedback.incorrect: Apply both orders to one point such as (1,2). Compare the two final coordinates.

sections.title: Reteach: use an input-output chain
sections.body: Write start → first image → final image. Never apply both rules to the original point.

items.prompt: Start at (−2,3). Reflect across the y-axis, then translate by ⟨1,−2⟩. Enter the final ordered pair.

feedback.correct: Your input-output chain preserves the specified order.
feedback.incorrect: First change only the x-coordinate for the reflection. Then add the translation vector to that image.

items.prompt: Map A(0,1), B(2,1), C(0,4) by a 180° rotation about the origin followed by translation ⟨−1,3⟩. Give the final vertices and one distance check.

feedback.correct: Your coordinates follow the ordered composition, and your invariant check supports the mapping.
feedback.incorrect: List the rotated vertices before translating. Then compare one side length before and after.

whatYouLearned: A transformation sequence must include complete defining information.
Distance and angle invariants help verify rigid-motion work.
lessonReview.courseProgress: This sample is based on Grade 10 Unit 2, lesson family 5. It does not change your production-course progress.
